chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from al-Halabi, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he was asked about a man who applies kohl while fasting, so he said:

"No, for I fear that its head [of the kohl] will enter [the throat]." These two reports and what follows their pattern refer to the kohl that contains musk or something with a sharp scent that enters the throat, for that is disliked. As for what is not like that, there is no harm in it. And that which indicates what we mentioned is what he narrated:

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no harm in it (permissible)

ai.seo_question: Does applying kohl break the fast in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the dislike (karahah) of kohl for the fasting person applies specifically to those with strong, penetrating scents like musk, which reach the throat, while ordinary kohl remains permissible. This ruling reflects the Shia juristic principle that the entry of substantial matter or distinct scent into the throat breaks the fast, distinguishing between medicinal/fragrant kohl and standard cosmetic application. The context highlights the nuanced approach of the Imams in balancing ritual purity with practical daily needs.
